source.title: Scaling Laws for Transfer
source.authors: Danny Hernandez; J. Kaplan; T. Henighan; Sam McCandlish

record.tranche_reason: The study measures transfer scaling in fine-tuning and qualifies the scope of the fitted law: the reported fit is for the low-data regime, and it breaks down in the high-data regime for some pre-training conditions.
record.gate_note: The study reports fitted transfer coefficients and high-data-regime outcomes. It also discusses prior results on architecture details, but does not test them. Its speculative few-shot estimates and cited downstream-task results are not independent tests of the versions here.
record.test_reason: The study tests whether scaling-law regularity carries over to unsupervised fine-tuning and transfer (V5). It trains transformers from scratch on Python, and pre-trained on text or text+code then fine-tuned on Python, across about 4 orders of magnitude of model size. It fits effective data transferred as a power law in fine-tuning data and parameters. This is a new training regime with its own result, so T3 rather than T5. The breakdown outside the low-data regime narrows the scope but is not the paper's main thrust.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that transfer is measurable across model sizes and scales predictably. In the low-data regime, effective data transferred follows a power law in fine-tuning data and parameters. β (0.38) is shared across pretraining mixes, and α measures the directed proximity of distributions. Pre-training effectively multiplies the fine-tuning data. The fit breaks down in the high-data regime, where small models show ossification.
record.recipe_differences: Rather than fitting held-out language-model loss directly against parameters, tokens, and compute, the study infers effective transferred Python data by matching held-out loss to same-size from-scratch models, then fits that quantity against fine-tuning data and parameter count. It focuses on unsupervised transfer fine-tuning.
record.method_sensitivity: The fit is reported for the low-data regime and breaks down outside it; the degree of breakdown differs between text-only and text-plus-code pretraining.

fits_no_version.finding: Ossification: small fine-tuned models stayed below from-scratch Python performance even with 10x or 100x D(N). Pre-training reduced effective data in the high-data regime.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Pre-training can harm converged performance of small models in the high-data regime (ossification).

fits_no_version.finding: Ignoring pre-training compute, fine-tuned models are more compute-efficient in the low-data regime and stay on the compute frontier more easily (Figs. 4, 7, 8).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Fine-tuning is more compute-efficient than training from scratch at small fine-tuning dataset sizes.

record.problems: The study measures transfer only for Python and unsupervised transformer fine-tuning. It reports limited hyperparameter tuning, notes that short runs on small datasets may be confounded by warmup, and says high-data effective-data estimates are poorly conditioned. Its attempted global fit to from-scratch Python runs was not good enough to support a unified predictive equation. Uncertainties are not reported for the listed fitted coefficients or high-data outcomes.
record.rows_left_out: No qualifying result rows were left out.

untested.parts: Other modalities, supervised or RL transfer, and target distributions other than Python. Non-transformer architectures.
Text pretraining loss versus N, D or compute over orders of magnitude. Only from-scratch Python runs are examined, and only per-dataset-size fits are shown.
No comparison of small-run extrapolations with measured large runs. The GPT-3-scale estimate is explicitly speculative.
Compute-optimal parameter/token allocation is not measured.
Depth, width and shape are not varied; the paper only cites prior work.
No downstream tasks are measured. The SuperGLUE few-shot argument is speculative and uses cited results.
Parameter counting, schedules and fitting methods are not varied to show effects on exponents.

missing.what: Global fit of Kaplan Eq. 1.5, L(N,D), to from-scratch Python runs was too poor to use. Per-dataset fits were power laws plus constants.

Fine-tuned Python loss versus model size at fixed DF keeps improving with a reduced slope, while from-scratch models plateau when data-limited. This is a direct loss-scaling result in the fine-tuning regime.

record.verdict_notes: r3/r4 were linked to V7, which concerns fitting and setup choices behind disagreement among published pretraining-loss laws. Breakdown of a transfer law outside its regime is a V5 scope result, so those links were moved. The V1 label rests on Appendix E, not on a row. Uncertainties are not reported for any fitted coefficient.

versions.untested_parts: It does not directly test held-out pretraining loss as a power law in parameters, tokens, or compute with the other quantities non-bottlenecked.
It does not compare predictions from small runs with measured losses of runs orders of magnitude larger. The GPT-3-scale estimate is explicitly speculative.
It discusses compute efficiency of fine-tuning but does not measure the loss-minimising parameter/token allocation as a function of a fixed compute budget.
Architecture details such as depth and width are not varied in this study.
Tests unsupervised transformer fine-tuning from text or text-plus-code to Python, not other modalities, supervised or reinforcement-learning settings, or a broad set of distribution pairs.
Held-out Python cross-entropy is measured, but downstream-task performance or its predictability from pretraining loss is not tested.

The study reports low- versus high-data-regime fit behavior and different fitting approaches, but does not systematically vary parameter-count conventions, training schedules, data, or fitting methods to quantify their effects on exponents.

relationships.condition: From-scratch Python transformers with hyperparameters not tuned for code
relationships.reason: Based on text (Appendix E, no row): Kaplan's joint L(N,D) form fit the from-scratch Python runs poorly. Per-dataset-size power-law-plus-constant fits worked (Fig. 3). The authors attribute the poor global fit to limited tuning.
relationships.display_finding: Kaplan's joint parameter–data formula fit poorly, attributed to limited tuning, while separate power-law-plus-constant fits worked at each dataset size.

relation.reason: Its own model and dataset sweeps test whether effective transfer follows a power law and identify where the fitted form breaks down.

tranche.reason: The study tests scaling regularity in a new setting: unsupervised transfer to Python, measured through effective transferred data. Its main contribution is a scaling result in that setting, with regime-dependent failures.

source_check.notes: The fitted transfer quantity is additional effective Python data, not loss directly. Appendix A uses a 99% intersection criterion for from-scratch models but 95% for fine-tuned models when estimating D(N).
